points: Management could confirm the 1,000-location milestone is on track for 2026, extending the 29.4% revenue growth trajectory into 2027 through new-shop contribution. This matters because expansion is the highest-conviction tailwind and the main driver of upside.

The call could update 2026 capex relative to the $200M falsifier threshold; if spending stays below that line while still adding stores, it would show disciplined capital intensity and protect cash flow. This matters because the bear case rests on overextension, and a controlled capex number would rebut it.

Q3 and Q4 2026 results could show new shops maturing fast enough to keep total revenue growth above 20% even with 3-5% same-store sales, extending the top-line momentum from Q4 2025. This matters because the long case relies on revenue and EBITDA growth, not just pricing.

The December Q4 2026 print could provide the first 2027 guidance and reiterate the path toward 4,000 units, shaping the 12-18 month setup. This matters because the rerating depends on investors believing the brand can scale nationally.

Coffee costs could remain below the 20% YoY increase falsifier, limiting further pressure on the 27% shop-revenue cost base into 2027. This matters because input-cost relief is the main lever that can turn recent EBITDA leverage into sustained margin expansion.

The balance sheet could keep a working capital ratio above the 1.5 falsifier, giving the company room to fund the 1,000-store push without dilutive financing or heavy debt. This matters because balance-sheet health underpins the aggressive expansion tailwind.

BJRI's October 28 print could offer a read-through on casual-dining traffic and pricing that helps judge whether BROS's Q3/Q4 same-store sales can hold the 3-5% guide. This matters because it is the next industry data point after BROS's own print and can confirm or challenge demand assumptions.
